items.title: Nasdaq Soars 1,471 Points as Jensen Huang Returns to Nvidia: Stock Market Today
items.summary:
Stocks jumped out of the gate Monday as Wall Street cheered reports that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO. Tech stocks have been tumbling since Huang stepped down earlier this month after it was revealed he had several extramarital affairs — at least one with a direct report and one with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

The recent tech-sector sell-off pulled the main market indexes into a correction last week — a drop of 10% from the most recent closing high — and had the Nasdaq Composite nearing a bear market .

But the Dow Jones Industrial Average (+3.0% at 49,595) and the S&P 500 (+4.7% at 7,237) exited correction territory Monday, while the Nasdaq (+6.5% to 24,089) has about 750 points left to go based on today's close.

Nvidia stock has best day in 23 years as Jensen Huang returns Nvidia stock soared 31.5% Monday — its biggest one-day percentage gain since May 9, 2003 — after the artificial intelligence (AI) bellwether's board of directors said Huang has been brought back as CEO. What's more, NVDA regained nearly $1 trillion ($954 billion to be exact) in market cap today — a record for any publicly traded U.S. company.

Track all markets on TradingView The call came following "a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang," Nvidia said in a press release . "In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."

President Donald Trump was quick to take credit…

The introduction of the first modern credit card in 1950 changed how Americans paid for purchases, while the polio vaccine, introduced in 1955, marked a major public health breakthrough. These milestones helped shape a new era of prosperity, convenience and opportunity.

items.title: Should You Skip Black Friday?
items.summary:
If you've been watching the early Black Friday deals roll out and are feeling less than impressed by them, you're not crazy. A slate of studies have emerged that all have similar findings: As much as 33% of the deals offered on Black Friday last year were "fake" deals. 

That is, the deal price was either the same or even higher than the price the product was selling for throughout most of the year. The teams behind these studies expect to see similar misleading deals plaguing this year's Black Friday . 

So, with so many fake Black Friday deals lurking in all these sales, should you skip shopping altogether? Not necessarily. Even with so many misleading discounts, the majority of deals were still legitimate and this can be a great opportunity to cross a lot of names off of your gift list for the holiday season. You just need to plan your deal-hunting accordingly and learn how to spot the difference between real and fake deals. 

A third of Black Friday deals aren't really saving you money Visualping , a website tracking tool that monitors price drops and other page changes, tracked 1,500 products across multiple categories during Black Friday last year. The company will be doing the same this year. Of those 1,500 products, 33% were cheaper before Black Friday than they were during the sales event. 

And it wasn't just a little more expensive either. On average, according to Visualping, these "fake" Black Friday deals were 37% more expensive than the product's lowest observed price. 

Wallethub conducted a similar study comparing Black Friday deal prices on Amazon with the…
items.t: Should You Skip Black Friday?

items.title: I-Bonds vs High-Yield Savings Accounts and CDs: Which is Better For You Now?
items.summary:
If you're looking for a safe place to grow your savings, a 5.5% interest rate on a savings bond may be worth considering. Series I savings bonds, also known as I-bonds , offer a way to earn interest while helping protect your savings against inflation. But how do they compare with more traditional savings options, such as certificates of deposit (CDs) and high-yield savings accounts?

Competitive one-year CDs are currently offering around 4.5% to 4.65% APY, while several high-yield savings accounts are paying around 4% or more. That means savers have several attractive options, each with different benefits and restrictions.

Before moving your money, here's how I-Bonds compare with CDs and high-yield savings accounts , and which option might make the most sense for your financial goals.

How does the new 5.5% I-Bond rate work? An I-Bond earns interest through two components: a fixed rate and an inflation-adjusted rate. The fixed rate is established when you purchase the bond and remains the same for the life of the bond, which could be up to 30 years.

The inflation-adjusted portion of earnings changes every six months and is based on the Consumer Price Index. Together, these two parts determine the bond's composite interest rate. The current I-bond rate of 5.5% was set on November 1, and it applies until April 30, 2027, at which point a new rate will be announced.

However, there's an important catch. The advertised 5.5% rate only applies to the first six months after purchasing an eligible I-bonds. After that, the inflation-adjusted portion resets, which means your total…
items.t: I-Bonds vs High-Yield Savings Accounts and CDs: Which is Better For You Now?

items.title: We're Gen Xers Secretly Paying My Parents’ Bills
items.summary:
Dear Wealth Wise : I'm 52, and my husband is 54. We make about $200K a year, but we have two kids in college and one is only a freshman. We still have a mortgage, live in a high-tax area, and can't move because my 80-something parents are 15 minutes away and need us. We have about $750K saved for retirement, no pensions. 

My parents live on Social Security plus my dad's small pension. I'm an only child and help support them. I buy groceries and don't ask for money, and my parents don't even realize we're paying some of their bills. The last time a plumber came, it cost $480. We paid him and told my parents it was $125. 

I'm not counting on an inheritance , especially if they need a nursing home, which they might eventually. Their paid-off house is probably worth $500K, and their savings are minimal. 

My husband and I probably provide more than $10K a year in support, which we could use for our own savings and to help pay for college. We don't want our parents to stress. But we're stressed. — Sandwiched Gen X 

Dear Sandwiched Gen X : When you're an only child, it's not unusual for the burden of caring for a parent to fall on you. It's also common to spend money in the course of caring for older parents.

AARP reports that family caregivers spend $11,508 a year on average. And while you and your spouse may be covering general living costs more than medical bills, it's clear you're spending money on your parents that you can't easily spare. That's true even though your $750K in retirement savings is well ahead of typical Gen X balances — for context, the average Gen X…
items.t: We're Gen Xers Secretly Paying My Parents’ Bills.

Even before the internet began siphoning off subscribers and ad revenue in the early 2000s, magazines had a high mortality rate, coming and going with changing tastes.

Print periodicals that have been continuously published for eight decades are pretty rare. items.title: Copper's Bull Case: 3 Less Obvious Stocks to Invest In
items.summary:
Copper is no longer an undiscovered investment theme.

The metal sits at the center of several enormous spending trends, including electric-grid expansion, electric vehicles, renewable power and industrial electrification. AI data centers add another source of demand, but they're only part of the story. 

Worldwide copper demand could rise about 50%, from roughly 28 million metric tons in 2025 to 42 million by 2040, according to recent S&P Global estimates.

The supply side may be even more important.

Copper mines are enormously capital intensive, and major projects can take 10 to 20 years to progress from discovery and development to production. Many of the world's largest mines have already been operating for decades, and aging mines can face declining ore grades, rising costs and increasing technical complexity.

Recent disruptions demonstrate just how difficult existing production can be to replace. A September 2025 mudflow at Freeport-McMoRan's Grasberg operation in Indonesia forced a broad suspension of mining operations at one of the world's largest copper deposits. Freeport expects the recovery process to continue into 2027.

Here's what they had to say.

Advice for younger people Save, save, and save some more. 

"Save! More! Money! You're lucky if your employer offers retirement investment accounts. If you're on your own, set one up at a low-cost mutual fund. Have, say, 10% swept out of every paycheck and then forget that money is there. Don't raid the funds if you need money, at least not until you have only two carrots left for dinner and the lights are out. If you're young and broke, you can recover, but not if you're old and broke."

items.title: Financial Adviser Fees: The View From a Consumer Advocate
items.summary:
One of the biggest myths about financial adviser fees is that the amount of money you have to invest drives the fee you'll pay for the advice. 

It's true that most advisers prefer to charge based on a percentage of your assets they manage, but the size of your portfolio doesn't necessarily reflect how much financial and tax planning you need or how complicated your financial life may be.

Someone with $500,000 in savings, several retirement accounts, rental properties and a complicated tax situation may need substantially more planning than someone with $2 million invested in a simple portfolio of index funds. 

The true story about adviser fees is that the price should reflect the work involved, not simply the size of your portfolio. Before comparing fees , you need to understand what you want an adviser to accomplish and what kind of relationship makes sense for you.

Different needs call for different kinds of advice One of the most important developments in financial advice is that consumers now have more choices in how they work with qualified, fee-only fiduciary advisers . 

Some want an adviser to directly manage their investments and provide ongoing financial planning Others want comprehensive planning advice but prefer to keep managing their own portfolios Still others just need help with one major decision About Adviser Intel

items.title: 5 Key Risks in the 10-Year Retirement Gap
items.summary:
If you're like most people nearing or in retirement , you've spent 20- to 30-plus years building your retirement savings. You've made sacrifices, saved diligently, invested consistently and watched your portfolio grow. 

But how many of us think about preparing for the next chapter? There's a transition on the horizon that doesn't happen automatically when you punch out for the last time and enter retirement. 

That transition should begin years before your final workday. The decisions you make in the five to 10 years before you retire, and in the first five years after, could shape your financial future more than any other period of your life.

I call this stretch of time the retirement danger gap, and it deserves far more attention than most people give it. It's the bridge between two very different phases: Growing your wealth and living on it while making sure it lasts. 

The ripple effect The gap shows up in the decisions you make during these years and in how those decisions ripple through the rest of your retirement . Making them without a trusted professional by your side can be the difference between a retirement that thrives and one that struggles.

When you were still working, you had two advantages: Time and paychecks. If the market had a rough spot when you were 40 years old, you could shrug it off, knowing you had plenty of time to recover any losses.

While many retirees are staying put in 2026, some plan to trade their larger homestead for simpler, easier-to-manage space.

According to Freddie Mac research , 66% of Baby Boomer homeowners (aged 62 to 80 in 2026) who are planning to move say they intend to downsize, joining the 36% of Boomer movers who have already scaled back.

Downsizing may offer some clear perks, like moving closer to family, ditching yard work, or freeing up home equity. Yet for longtime homeowners sitting on decades of appreciated value, the biggest financial hurdle may lie in the U.S. tax code.

That's because IRS rules hold several quiet traps that can turn a familial home sale into an unexpected tax bill . For instance, claiming a home office deduction years ago can erase tens of thousands of dollars in tax-free capital gains.

So before you put a "for sale" sign in your yard, watch out for these five hidden downsizing tax traps in 2026.

1. Missing the two-year deadline for surviving spouses 

(Image credit: Getty Images) Losing a spouse is overwhelming, and rushing into a move is often the last thing on a grieving partner's mind. Yet waiting too long to sell can unfortunately trigger what some tax pros call the " widow's tax penalty ."

When married couples sell a primary residence, federal rules typically allow a capital gains tax exclusion of up to $500,000. Many retirees assume they can wait several years after a spouse passes away to downsize, not realizing half of that tax shield expires on a deadline. Under IRS rules , an unmarried surviving spouse only keeps the full $500,000 home sale…
items.t: 5 Hidden Tax Traps That Cost Retirees When Downsizing

items.title: The 5-Year Retirement Shortfall Awaiting the Average American
items.summary:
Planning for only average conditions, with little room for error, can sink any journey. Sometimes tragically so, as with the ill-fated Robert Falcon Scott expedition racing to be first to the South Pole. Beset by blizzards and low on fuel, Scott and his crew perished only 11 miles short of their next supply station.

Many Americans may be facing their own devastating shortfall in the journey known as retirement, according to a recent survey. The life insurance company Ethos asked 1,000 Americans about their retirement savings and found the average American wants to live to 88 but says their savings can only support them to 83 .

The good news is that this five-year retirement gap between lifespan and savings isn't set in stone. Experts suggest a mix of moves — some that grow your assets, others that make them last longer — can help keep your savings from running out before you do.

Here are five key strategies to get started.

1. Plan for living longer than you think The saying, "no one wants to be average," could actually be the perfect attitude for your retirement plan.

As Matthew Chancey, CFP® and founder of Tax Alpha Companies , points out, "The real shortfall usually starts with planning to the average." He explains that Social Security Administration actuaries estimate a man who is 65 today will live to about 83, on average, and a woman to about 86. Because those are averages, roughly half of people live longer. So a plan built to the average age is a plan that runs out about half the time.

That's why some advisers suggest building a plan around living to 90 or…
items.t: The 5-Year Retirement Shortfall Awaiting the Average American

items.title: The Hardest Retirement Skill: Spending What You Saved
items.summary:
For the 30 or 40 years or more of our working lives, the instructions are straightforward: Save. Invest. Max out what you can. Don't touch the retirement accounts. Watch the balances grow.

Then retirement arrives and the instructions suddenly reverse: Now start spending the money.

For disciplined savers, that shift can be harder than it sounds. Watching a balance decline can feel like failure, even when spending that money is exactly what your financial plan says you can afford to do. Spending is exactly what you've been saving for.

A successful retirement plan gives you the financial strategy to build your retirement savings and the confidence to spend that money so you can enjoy this chapter of your life. Your nest egg may be ready, but your mindset might need to catch up. Here's how to get in the right retirement spending headspace.

1. Start with your life, not your number If someone told me, "I have $1 million saved , so I'm ready to retire," my response would be, "Tell me about your life, not just your account balances." 

A number is just a number. What you really need to know is what you want your money to do for you. Money is a tool.

items.title: Waiting Until Your 70s for RMDs Can Spring a Pricey Tax Surprise
items.summary:
Required minimum distributions (RMDs) have a way of feeling like a problem for later. You are not required to take them yet, the account is growing nicely, and there is always next year to think about it. 

That comfort is exactly the trap. The cost of treating RMDs as a future concern is not paid when they begin. It is paid in the years you spent ignoring them, when you could have been acting and chose to wait. 

By the time the distributions arrive, the most valuable planning years are already behind you.

What RMDs actually are Once you reach a certain age, the IRS stops letting your tax-deferred accounts grow untouched. You must begin withdrawing a calculated amount each year from accounts like traditional IRAs and 401(k)s , whether you need the money or not, and each withdrawal is taxed as ordinary income. 

For 2026, the age at which RMDs generally begin is 73. The amount is determined by your account balance and an IRS life expectancy factor , and it rises as a percentage of the balance as you age.

The penalty for getting it wrong is steep. Miss an RMD and the shortfall can be hit with a penalty of 25%, reduced to 10% if you correct it promptly. That alone is reason enough to take them seriously. 

But the larger cost is not the penalty. It is what compounds quietly in the years before RMDs ever start.

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.
